newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's Stoyanov owes presidency to deep crisis.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's Stoyanov owes presidency to deep crisis.

text.p: Petar Stoyanov, who scored a resounding victory in Sunday's presidential election, owes his meteoric political rise to Bulgaria's deep economic malaise and the anti-communist opposition's new-found unity.

The 44-year-old lawyer, virtually unknown outside his Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) party six months ago, won around 60 percent of the votes cast, trouncing his rival Ivan Marazov of the governing Socialist Party (BSP).

Bulgarians, battered by soaring prices, bank closures and fears of bread and fuel shortages this winter, expressed their anger with Prime Minister Zhan Videnov's government by voting for a fresh face as their head of state.
But Stoyanov, tall, athletic and bespectacled, sent a conciliatory message to Videnov in a news conference on Sunday night at Sofia's huge communist-era Palace of Culture.
"I want to be the president of all Bulgarians," he said.
Stoyanov avoided direct criticism of the cabinet and suggested a National Salvation Council of experts and respected public figures to advise on how to tackle the crisis.
"My first concern is ensuring that Bulgarians survive the winter, which is going to be very tough," he said.

Under Bulgaria's post-communist constitution, the presidency is a largely ceremonial post but the scale of Stoyanov's victory has put the government on the defensive and could trigger new rifts within the ruling party.

Stoyanov, a pro-market liberal, reiterated his strong support for binding Bulgaria more closely to Western Europe. The small Balkan country has continued looking towards Moscow, its historic patron, even after the fall of communism.
"Political independence and economic stability come through integration into the European Union and the Atlantic Alliance," Stoyanov said.
He made pre-election visits to Germany, where he met Chancellor Helmut Kohl, and to Poland, whose increasing prosperity under a moderate leftist government contrasts strongly with Bulgaria's turmoil.

Stoyanov burst onto the political centre-stage in June when he defeated President Zhelyu Zhelev in a U.S.-style primary election designed to select a single presidential candidate for the traditionally fractious anti-communist opposition.
Zhelev, also a liberal, bowed out of the contest and will formally hand over the reins of office to Stoyanov in January.
Stoyanov made a particular effort to appeal to young voters and was endorsed by Bulgaria's international soccer stars Hristo Stoichkov and Emil Kostadinov.
A professional politician, Stoyanov offers a younger, slicker image after Zhelev, a former dissident academic who always looked slightly ill at ease in a suit.
Stoyanov's vigorous, straightforward way of speaking also contrasts with Zhelev's rambling, philosophical style.
Stoyanov was born on May 25, 1952 in Plovdiv and studied law at Sofia University. He practised law in Plovdiv and became deputy justice minister in the first UDF government from 1991 to 1992.
A former volleyball player, he is married with two children. His wife, also a lawyer by training, is a diplomat at the Bulgarian embassy in London.
Antonina Stoyanova, who has said she would return to Sofia if her husband became president, told Sunday's Troud newspaper she hates being compared to U.S. first lady Hillary Clinton.
"The president's wife should not be involved in politics. After all, the people vote for Petar, not for me," she said.
